title: Nested homogeneous quotients, translated fibres and equal-dimension finiteness
statement:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $G$ be a smooth connected affine group scheme of finite type over $k$ [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and let $H\subseteq J\subseteq G$ be closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup], with no smoothness or connectedness assumption on $H$ or $J$. Quotients mean the separated finite-type schemes representing the fppf coset sheaves of [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homogeneous-quotient]. There is a canonical faithfully flat morphism of finite presentation
$$\pi:G/H\longrightarrow G/J,\qquad gH\longmapsto gJ.$$
For the quotient map $q_J:G\to G/J$ there is a canonical isomorphism over $G$
$$G\times_k(J/H)\xrightarrow{\sim}G\times_{G/J}(G/H),\qquad(g,jH)\longmapsto(g,gjH).$$
Thus the fibre over $q_J(g)$, for $g\in G(k)$, is isomorphic to $J/H$ by $jH\mapsto gjH$. If $\dim H=\dim J$, then $\pi$ is finite. Dimensions mean topological Krull dimension [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. In particular, for an arbitrary closed subgroup $J\subseteq G$, let $J^0$ denote the open and closed identity component, with its open-subscheme structure, and let $H=(J^0)_{\mathrm{red}}$ be its reduction (quotienting the structure sheaf by the ideal of nilpotent sections) [lem-sfb-locally-algebraic-group-identity-component, def-weil-pbc-scheme-reduction]. Then $H$ is smooth and connected, $\dim H=\dim J$, and $G/H\to G/J$ is finite and faithfully flat. Here finite and morphism properties have the meanings of [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism, def-pc-morphism-conventions], and the displayed products have the meaning of [def-pc-fibre-product].

source.place: Proposition 7.15 and its Cartesian square, printed pp.142--143; Remark 7.16(a),(b), printed p.143; Proposition 5.23, printed p.104. The map direction is the one in the Cartesian square and Remark 7.16(b), correcting the reversed arrow in the second sentence of Proposition 7.15.

proof.text: Apply the homogeneous-quotient theorem to $(G,H)$, $(G,J)$ and $(J,H)$, obtaining $X=G/H$, $Y=G/J$, $Z=J/H$ and quotient maps $q_H,q_J,r$. The closed subgroups are separated and finite type: on a finite affine cover of the affine finite-type group $G$, their rings are quotients of the chart rings. The theorem explicitly allows nonsmooth and disconnected subgroups. Each quotient map is flat, surjective and of finite presentation, hence is a singleton fpqc cover by the covering definition. Also $Z\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is flat, since every vector space has a basis and tensoring with it is a direct sum of identity functors. It is locally of finite presentation by the locally-Noetherian-base lemma: the only ideals of $k$ are $(0)$ and $k$, so $\operatorname{Spec}k$ is Noetherian. It is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, being separated and finite type.

source.place: Proposition 7.15 setup; Theorem 5.28; finite-presentation input Stacks Tag 01TX (lemma-noetherian-finite-type-finite-presentation)

proof.text: On $G\times_XG$ the universal pair $(a,b)$ satisfies $a^{-1}b\in H$, by the coset-fibre clause of the quotient theorem. Since $H\subseteq J$, the same clause for $q_J$ gives $q_J(a)=q_J(b)$. The representable fpqc descent theorem, applied to the singleton $q_H:G\to X$, therefore gives a unique $\pi:X\to Y$ with $\pi q_H=q_J$. This constructs the canonical map, with the stipulated formula on cosets, without assuming that every section of $X$ lifts globally to $G$.

source.place: Proposition 5.21 and Proposition 7.15: descend q_J along q_H; representable descent Stacks Tag 023Q (lemma-fpqc-universal-effective-epimorphisms)

proof.text: The map $(g,j)\mapsto(g,q_H(gj))$ from $G\times_kJ$ lands in $G\times_YX$, since $q_J(gj)=q_J(g)$. Along the fpqc cover $1_G\times r$ of $G\times_kZ$, two representatives of the second coordinate differ by right multiplication by $h\in H$, and $q_H(gjh)=q_H(gj)$. Representable descent gives $\Phi:G\times_kZ\to G\times_YX$. For its inverse, take a $T$-section $(g,x)$ of the latter scheme and pull back $q_H$ along $x$ to an fpqc cover $T'\to T$. There $x=q_H(a)$; equality $q_J(a)=q_J(g)$ implies $j=g^{-1}a\in J(T')$ by the coset-fibre clause for $J$. On $T'\times_TT'$, two lifts satisfy $a_2=a_1h$ for some $h\in H$, so $r(g^{-1}a_2)=r(g^{-1}a_1)$. Representable descent glues this section to $z:T\to Z$. It is independent of the lift and of further covers by the same uniqueness. Thus $(g,x)\mapsto(g,z)$ is natural in $T$, and its composites with $\Phi$ are identities: on local representatives they are $g^{-1}(gj)=j$ and $g(g^{-1}a)=a$. Taking universal sections gives inverse scheme morphisms. This proves the displayed isomorphism over $G$, also on nonreduced test schemes.

source.place: Proposition 7.15 Cartesian square: explicit construction and inverse after fpqc local lifts; Stacks Tag 023Q for gluing

proof.text: By Step 3, the pullback of $\pi$ along $q_J$ is the projection $G\times_kZ\to G$. It is flat and locally of finite presentation by base change of the structure morphism of $Z$, using Step 1. Apply fpqc descent of flatness and of local finite presentation to the singleton cover $q_J$; hence $\pi$ has both properties. It is surjective because $q_J=\pi q_H$ is surjective: every point of $Y$ is the image of some point of $G$, hence of its image in $X$. Finally $X$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated and $Y$ is quasi-separated, since both are separated finite-type $k$-schemes. The qcqs permanence statement shows that $\pi$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. Together with local finite presentation, this proves finite presentation.

For $g\in G(k)$ pull the isomorphism $\Phi$ back along $g:\operatorname{Spec}k\to G$. Its left side becomes $Z$ and its right side is $X\times_{Y,q_J(g)}\operatorname{Spec}k$, by the defining universal property of fibre products. The resulting map is exactly $jH\mapsto gjH$, with inverse obtained by multiplication by $g^{-1}$ as in Step 3. This identifies the whole fibre scheme, not just its set of $k$-points.

source.place: Remark 7.16(a), translated by g; base change of the Proposition 7.15 Cartesian square

proof.text: Assume $\dim H=\dim J$. Apply the homogeneous-quotient dimension formula with $A=J$ and $L=H$: $\dim J=\dim H+\dim Z$, with finite nonnegative integer dimensions, so $\dim Z=0$. By the local-ring description of scheme dimension, every local ring of $Z$ has Krull dimension at most $0$, so $Z$ has dimension at most $0$ in the local-ring sense of the next lemma. The zero-dimensional finite-type scheme lemma makes $Z\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ finite. Its base change $G\times_kZ\to G$ is finite by finite-morphism permanence. Step 3 identifies this map with the pullback of $\pi$ along the fpqc singleton $q_J$. Fpqc descent of finite morphisms now makes $\pi$ finite. This argument retains infinitesimal structure in $H$, $J$ and $Z$; it uses no smoothness of them.

source.place: Proposition 5.23 and Remark 7.16(b); Stacks Tag 06LH (lemma-algebraic-scheme-dim-0), Tag 02LA (lemma-descending-property-finite); Stacks Tag 04MU (properties-lemma-dimension) for the two dimension notions

proof.text: For an arbitrary $J$, apply the identity-component statement to $J$: its clopen subgroup $J^0$ has reduction $H$ which is a smooth connected finite-type subgroup and has the same underlying space as $J^0$. The inclusion $H\hookrightarrow J$ is closed: on the clopen decomposition $J=J^0\amalg(J\setminus J^0)$ its defining ideal is the nilradical on the first piece and the unit ideal on the second piece. At the identity the local rings of $J$ and its open subscheme $J^0$ agree. The group-identity local-dimension lemma, applied separately to $J$ and $J^0$, therefore gives $\dim J=\dim\mathcal O_{J,e}=\dim\mathcal O_{J^0,e}=\dim J^0$. The equality of underlying spaces gives $\dim H=\dim J^0$. Thus $\dim H=\dim J$, and Steps 4 and 6 give the required finite faithfully flat map $G/H\to G/J$.
